chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter opens with Estu's question about a lakh varieties of rice and keeps it open until the student has climbed to one lakh and worked out the days in a lifetime. Every story is a video that ends on a question the student answers before the idea is named, and an interactive tool appears only where handling the numbers is the idea itself.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves Estu's question open. The word lakh is built up from the largest five-digit number before anyone is told how big it is, and the answer comes only after the student has compared a lifetime of days with one lakh.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: concept videos, one per concept, a closing practice concept (with a tool where handling the numbers is the concept), then the book's Figure it Out questions in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

points.title: Feel the size, then name it
points.text: A large number is compared with something familiar: a building, a lifetime, a city. Lakh, crore, arab, million and billion are placed on one picture with the zeros counted.

points.title: Estimate, then calculate
points.text: Rounding, benchmarks and what-if questions with stated assumptions are used before and after the exact calculation, so the student can tell if an answer is reasonable.

concepts.concept_name: A lakh varieties of rice and Estu's question

content.text:
1.1 A Lakh Varieties!
Eshwarappa is a farmer in Chintamani, a town in Karnataka. He visits the market regularly to buy seeds for his rice field. During one such visit he overheard a conversation between Ramanna and Lakshmamma. Ramanna said, "Earlier our country had about a lakh varieties of rice. Farmers used to preserve different varieties of seeds and use them to grow rice. Now, we only have a handful of varieties. Also, farmers have to come to the market to buy seeds".
Lakshmamma said, "There is a seed bank near my house. So far, they have collected about a hundred indigenous varieties of rice seeds from different places. You can also buy seeds from there."
You may have heard the word 'lakh' before. Do you know how big one lakh is? Let us find out.
Eshwarappa shared this incident with his daughter Roxie and son Estu.
Estu was surprised to know that there were about one lakh varieties of rice in this country. He wondered "One lakh! So far I have only tasted 3 varieties. If we tried a new variety each day, would we even come close to tasting all the varieties in a lifetime of 100 years?"
What do you think? Guess.

content.text:
1. Picture a seed bank with jars of rice seeds, each jar a different variety. The country once had about a lakh of them.
2. Estu has tasted 3 varieties. He asks what happens if he tries a new variety every single day for 100 years.
3. Make a guess before the next step: would 100 years of tasting come close to one lakh varieties?

3. Keep this question in mind: the next topic builds up to one lakh and then answers it.

concepts.concept_name: From 999 up to one lakh

content.text:
But how much is one lakh? Observe the pattern and fill in the boxes given below.
The largest 3-digit number is 999. The smallest 4-digit number is __. The largest 4-digit number is __. The smallest 5-digit number is __. The largest 5-digit number is __. The smallest 6-digit number is 1,00,000.
99,995, 99,996, 99,998 ... each step is +1.
1,00,000 is read as "One Lakh".

content.text:
Worked example: Fill in the pattern: the largest 3-digit number is 999. Give the smallest 4-digit, the largest 4-digit, the smallest 5-digit, the largest 5-digit and the smallest 6-digit number.
1. 999 + 1 = 1000, the smallest 4-digit number.
2. The largest 4-digit number is 9999.
3. 9999 + 1 = 10,000, the smallest 5-digit number.
4. The largest 5-digit number is 99,999.
5. 99,999 + 1 = 1,00,000, the smallest 6-digit number, read as one lakh.
Answer: 1000, 9999, 10,000, 99,999 and 1,00,000 (one lakh)

concepts.concept_name: Days in a lifetime and a lakh varieties

content.text:
Roxie and Estu found that if they ate one variety of rice a day, they would come nowhere close to a lakh in a lifetime! Roxie suggests, "What if we ate 2 varieties of rice every day? Would we then be able to eat 1 lakh varieties of rice in 100 years?"
What if a person ate 3 varieties of rice every day? Will they be able to taste all the lakh varieties in a 100 year lifetime? Find out.
Estu said, "We know how many days there are in a year, 365, if we ignore leap years. If we live for y years, the number of days in our lifetime will be 365 × y."
Choose a number for y. How close to one lakh is the number of days in y years, for the y of your choice?

1. Predict first: in 100 years, will one variety a day come close to one lakh? Will three a day reach it?
2. Days in y years: 365 × y. Varieties tasted: days × varieties a day.
3. Choose your own y. For y = 50 the days are 365 × 50 = 18,250, which is 81,750 short of one lakh.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the days in 100 years. Then find the varieties tasted in 100 years at one, two and three varieties a day, and compare each with one lakh.
1. Days in 100 years: 365 × 100 = 36,500.
2. One a day: 36,500 varieties.
3. Two a day: 36,500 × 2 = 73,000 varieties.
4. Three a day: 36,500 × 3 = 1,09,500 varieties.
5. 1,00,000 − 73,000 = 27,000, so two a day falls short of one lakh.
6. 1,09,500 − 1,00,000 = 9,500, so three a day passes one lakh.
Answer: 36,500; 73,000; 1,09,500. Only three varieties a day passes one lakh.

concepts.concept_name: Practice: how far from one lakh

content.text:
To see how far a number is below one lakh, subtract it from 1,00,000.
To see how far it is above one lakh, subtract 1,00,000 from it.
The change between two numbers is the larger one minus the smaller one.

tool_config.title: Lakh Ruler
tool_config.idea: A number can be placed on a ruler marked at one lakh; the gap to the mark is found by subtracting the smaller from the larger, and the change between two numbers is the larger minus the smaller.
tool_config.screen: A horizontal ruler from 0 to 2,00,000 with a bold mark at 1,00,000; a draggable pointer with a number box; a gap bar that grows between the pointer and the mark and says less than or more than one lakh; a second pointer for finding the change between two numbers.
student_does: Predict whether the number is below or above one lakh, then drag the pointer to it.
Read the gap bar and type how far the number is from one lakh.
Add a second pointer and type the change between the two numbers.
Press Check to see the subtraction written out.
challenges: Place 75,000 and find how much less than one lakh it is (25,000).
Place 1,06,000 and find how much more than one lakh it is (6,000).
Place both and find the change from 75,000 to 1,06,000 (31,000).
Place 99,500 and find the gap to one lakh (500).
Place 1,25,000 and find the gap to one lakh (25,000).
Place 36,500 and 1,09,500 and find which is closer to one lakh (1,09,500, gap 9,500).
feedback: A wrong gap shows the subtraction with the larger number first, so the order is clear.
A pointer on the wrong side of the mark turns the gap bar to the other colour and names less than or more than.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q1 (Chintamani in 2011)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q1 (Chintamani in 2011): According to the 2011 Census, the population of the town of Chintamani was about 75,000. How much less than one lakh is 75,000?
1. One lakh is 1,00,000.
2. 1,00,000 − 75,000 = 25,000.
Answer: 75,000 is 25,000 less than one lakh

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q3 (growth of Chintamani)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q3 (growth of Chintamani): By how much did the population of Chintamani increase from 2011 to 2024?
1. In 2011 the population was about 75,000 and in 2024 it is 1,06,000.
2. The increase is the later value minus the earlier value.
3. 1,06,000 − 75,000 = 31,000.
4. Check: 25,000 below one lakh and 6,000 above it give 25,000 + 6,000 = 31,000.
Answer: The population increased by 31,000

concepts.concept_name: Comparing with Somu's building

content.text:
Getting a Feel of Large Numbers
You may have come across interesting facts like these:
The world's tallest statue is the 'Statue of Unity' in Gujarat depicting Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Its height is about 180 metres.
Kunchikal waterfall in Karnataka is said to drop from a height of about 450 metres.
It is not always easy to get a sense of how big these measurements are. But, we can get a better sense of their size when we compare them with something familiar. Let us see an example.
Look at the picture on the right. Somu is 1 metre tall. If each floor is about four times his height, what is the approximate height of the building?
Which is taller, The Statue of Unity or this building? How much taller?
We can see that the height of the Statue of Unity is close to 4 times the height of Somu's building.
How much taller is the Kunchikal waterfall than Somu's building?
How many floors should Somu's building have to be as high as the waterfall?

2. Predict first: will the building be taller than the statue, which is 180 metres?
3. One floor is 4 m, so 10 floors are 40 m. Compare each tall thing with 40 m.
4. Floors needed for a height: divide the height by 4 m, the height of one floor.

content.text:
Worked example: Somu is 1 m tall and each floor is about 4 m. The picture shows 10 floors. Find the height of the building, how much taller the Statue of Unity (180 m) and the Kunchikal waterfall (450 m) are, and how many floors match the waterfall.
1. One floor is 4 × 1 = 4 m, so 10 floors are 10 × 4 = 40 m.
2. Statue of Unity: 180 − 40 = 140 m taller than the building.
3. Kunchikal waterfall: 450 − 40 = 410 m taller than the building.
4. Floors for 450 m: 450 ÷ 4 is 112.5, so about 113 floors.
5. The statue is 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5 times the building, a little more than 4 times.
Answer: The building is 40 m; the statue is 140 m taller; the waterfall is 410 m taller; about 113 floors

concepts.concept_name: Is one lakh a very large number

content.text:
Is One Lakh a Very Large Number?
Eshwarappa asked Roxie and Estu, "Is a lakh big or small?"
Roxie feels that 1 lakh is a large number: "We had one lakh varieties of rice, that is a lot." "Living 1 lakh days would mean living for 274 years, that is a really long time!" "If 1 lakh people stood shoulder to shoulder in a line they could stretch as far as 38 kilometres."
Estu, however, thinks it is not that big: "Do you know that the cricket stadium in Ahmedabad has a seating capacity of more than 1 lakh? One lakh people in such a small area!" "Most humans have 80,000 to 1,20,000 hairs on their heads. Imagine, 1 lakh hairs fit in such a tiny space!" "I heard that there are some species of fish where a female fish can lay almost one lakh eggs at once very comfortably. Some even lay tens of lakhs of eggs at a time."
How do you view a lakh, is a lakh big or small?
Note to the Teacher: Encourage students to make connections between these facts. For example, can the whole population of Chintamani fit in the stadium? How can we imagine the line of 38 km, having a lakh people, sitting next to each other in the stadium?

1. Predict first: do you think a lakh days is closer to 27 years or to 274 years?
2. Roxie compares a lakh with a lifetime and a long line, so it looks large. Estu compares it with a stadium, a head of hair and fish eggs, so it looks small.
3. A lakh is big or small depending on what it is compared with. Check each claim with a calculation.

content.text:
Worked example: Check Roxie's two claims: 1 lakh days is about 274 years, and 1 lakh people shoulder to shoulder stretch about 38 km. Assume a person is 38 cm wide. Is a lakh big or small?
1. Years in 1 lakh days: 1,00,000 ÷ 365 is about 274 years.
2. Line of people: 1,00,000 × 38 = 38,00,000 cm.
3. 38,00,000 ÷ 100 = 38,000 m, and 38,000 ÷ 1000 = 38 km.
4. Both claims hold, so a lakh days and a lakh people in a row are long.
5. A lakh seats in a stadium or a lakh hairs on a head fit in a small space, so a lakh can look small.
6. So a lakh is big or small depending on what it is compared with.
Answer: About 274 years and 38 km; a lakh is big or small depending on the comparison

media.title: Is a lakh a big number or a small one?
media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The video checks two claims about a lakh: a lakh days is a very long time and a lakh people in a row stretch very far. It then hears the other side from the stadium and the hairs on a head. Keeko raises a hand, thinking the line of people is thirty eight lakh metres long.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: whether a lakh is big or small depends on what it is compared with, and a claim is checked by turning it into a calculation with the right units. Ask the class to name the unit of each answer before moving on. Watch for students who leave a length in centimetres but call it metres.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the height of a ten-floor building from the height of one floor, find how much taller a statue and a waterfall are, and count the floors needed to match the waterfall.
Students check Roxie's lakh-days and lakh-people claims by calculation, quote Estu's reasons that a lakh can look small, and say why big or small depends on the comparison.
Students compare a tall height with a building of floors, say how many times taller it is, and judge a big number against a real thing.

concepts.concept_name: Number names with lakhs

content.text:
Reading and Writing Numbers
We have already been using commas for 5-digit numbers like 45,830 in the Indian place value system. As numbers grow bigger, using commas helps in reading the numbers easily. We use a comma in between the digits representing the "ten thousands" place and the "one lakh" place as you have seen just before (1,00,000).
The number name of 12,78,830 is twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty. Similarly, the number 15,75,000 in words is fifteen lakh seventy five thousand.
Write each of the numbers given below in words: (a) 3,00,600 (b) 5,04,085 (c) 27,30,000 (d) 70,53,138

content.text:
Worked example: Write 12,78,830 and the numbers (a) 3,00,600 and (b) 5,04,085 in words.
1. 12,78,830: 12 lakh, 78 thousand, 8 hundreds and 30.
2. So 12,78,830 is twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty.
3. (a) 3,00,600: 3 lakh, 00 thousand, 600. The zero thousands are not said.
4. (a) is three lakh six hundred.
5. (b) 5,04,085: 5 lakh, 04 thousand, 085.
6. (b) is five lakh four thousand eighty five.
Answer: Twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty; (a) three lakh six hundred; (b) five lakh four thousand eighty five

media.title: Comma Ladder

tool_config.title: Comma Ladder
tool_config.idea: Commas mark groups of digits from the right: thousands, then lakhs, then crores in the Indian system. Placing commas first makes a long number easy to read and to write in words.
tool_config.screen: A row of digit boxes for a number up to 10 digits; a ladder of place names under it (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, ten lakhs, crores, ten crores, arabs); comma markers the student drags; a words line that fills as the commas are placed.
student_does: Predict where the first comma will go.
Drag the comma markers between the digit boxes, from the right.
Read the words line that fills in and fix any wrong group.
Switch to numerals: type a number written in words and see the digits and commas.
challenges: Place commas in 4,50,678 and read it (four lakh fifty thousand six hundred seventy eight).
Place commas in 27,05,300 (twenty seven lakh five thousand three hundred).
Place commas in 3,08,00,000 (three crore eight lakh).
Write 90,00,500 in words (ninety lakh five hundred).

content.text:
1.2 Land of Tens
In the Land of Tens, there are special calculators with special buttons.
1. The Thoughtful Thousands only has a +1000 button. How many times should it be pressed to show: (a) Three thousand? 3 times (b) 10,000? (c) Fifty three thousand? (d) 90,000? (e) One Lakh? (f) ? 153 times (g) How many thousands are required to make one lakh?

content.text:
Worked example: Thoughtful Thousands has only a +1000 button. Find the presses for (a) 3000, (b) 10,000, (c) 53,000, (d) 90,000, (e) one lakh, (f) the number shown by 153 presses, and (g) the thousands in one lakh.
1. (a) 3000 ÷ 1000 = 3 presses.
2. (b) 10,000 ÷ 1000 = 10 presses.
3. (c) 53,000 ÷ 1000 = 53 presses.
4. (d) 90,000 ÷ 1000 = 90 presses.
5. (e) 1,00,000 ÷ 1000 = 100 presses.
6. (f) 153 × 1000 = 1,53,000.
7. (g) One lakh has 100 thousands.
Answer: (a) 3 (b) 10 (c) 53 (d) 90 (e) 100 (f) 1,53,000 (g) 100

content.text:
Worked example: Tedious Tens has only a +10 button. Find the presses for (a) 500, (b) 780, (c) 1000, (d) 3700, (e) 10,000, (f) one lakh, and the number shown by (g) 435 presses.
1. (a) 500 ÷ 10 = 50 presses.
2. (b) 780 ÷ 10 = 78 presses.
3. (c) 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 presses.
4. (d) 3700 ÷ 10 = 370 presses.
5. (e) 10,000 ÷ 10 = 1000 presses.
6. (f) 1,00,000 ÷ 10 = 10,000 presses.
7. (g) 435 × 10 = 4350.
Answer: (a) 50 (b) 78 (c) 100 (d) 370 (e) 1000 (f) 10,000 (g) 4350

Worked example: Handy Hundreds has only a +100 button. Find the presses for (a) 400, (b) 3,700, (c) 10,000, (d) 53,000, (e) 90,000, (f) 97,600, (g) 1,00,000, the number shown by (h) 582 presses, the hundreds in (i) ten thousand and (j) one lakh, and decide the statement in (k).

2. (b) 3700 ÷ 100 = 37 presses.
3. (c) 10,000 ÷ 100 = 100 presses.
4. (d) 53,000 ÷ 100 = 530 presses.
5. (e) 90,000 ÷ 100 = 900 presses.
6. (f) 97,600 ÷ 100 = 976 presses.
7. (g) 1,00,000 ÷ 100 = 1000 presses.
8. (h) 582 × 100 = 58,200.
9. (i) Ten thousand has 100 hundreds.
10. (j) One lakh has 1000 hundreds.

Answer: (a) 4 (b) 37 (c) 100 (d) 530 (e) 900 (f) 976 (g) 1000 (h) 58,200 (i) 100 (j) 1000 (k) No

media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A calculator in the Land of Tens has only a plus one thousand button. The video finds the presses for several numbers by dividing by one thousand, and shows what one hundred fifty three presses make. Keeko raises a hand, thinking that ten presses make a lakh.

concepts.concept_name: Many ways to make a number

content.text:
4. Creative Chitti is a different kind of calculator. It has the following buttons: +1, +10, +100, +1000, +10000, +100000 and +1000000. It always has multiple ways of doing things. "How so?", you might ask.
To get the number 321, it presses +10 thirty two times and +1 once. Will it get 321? Alternatively, it can press +100 two times and +10 twelve times and +1 once.
5. Two of the many different ways to get 5072 are shown below. These two ways can be expressed as: (a) (50 × 100) + (7 × 10) + (2 × 1) = 5072 (b) (3 × 1000) + (20 × 100) + (72 × 1) = 5072
Find a different way to get 5072 and write an expression for the same.

content.text:
Worked example: Two ways to get 5072 are (50 × 100) + (7 × 10) + (2 × 1) and (3 × 1000) + (20 × 100) + (72 × 1). Find a different way and write its expression.
1. Start from 5072 = 5000 + 70 + 2.
2. Use 4 presses of +1000 and trade the last 1000 for 10 presses of +100.
3. (4 × 1000) + (10 × 100) + (7 × 10) + (2 × 1) = 4000 + 1000 + 70 + 2 = 5072.
4. That is 4 + 10 + 7 + 2 = 23 presses; the sum is 5072, so the way works.
Answer: (4 × 1000) + (10 × 100) + (7 × 10) + (2 × 1) = 5072

concepts.concept_name: Chitti's challenges

content.text:
Creative Chitti has some questions for you:
(a) You have to make exactly 30 button presses. What is the largest 3-digit number you can make? What is the smallest 3-digit number you can make?
(b) 997 can be made using 25 clicks. Can you make 997 with a different number of clicks?
Create questions like these and challenge your classmates.

(a) You have to make exactly 30 button presses. What is the largest 3-digit number you can make? What is the smallest 3-digit number you can make?

Create questions like these and challenge your classmates.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 997 takes 9 + 9 + 7 = 25 presses. If one press of +100 is swapped for ten presses of +10, do the presses go up or down?
2. A swap of one press for ten presses changes the count by 9. So the presses are the digit sum plus a multiple of 9.
3. For exactly 30 presses the gap from the digit sum must be a multiple of 9.

content.text:
Worked example: 997 can be made with 25 presses. Make 997 with a different number of presses. Then find the largest and the smallest 3-digit number that can be made with exactly 30 presses.
1. 997 = (9 × 100) + (9 × 10) + (7 × 1) takes 9 + 9 + 7 = 25 presses.
2. Trade one +100 press for ten +10 presses: (8 × 100) + (19 × 10) + (7 × 1) = 997.
3. That takes 8 + 19 + 7 = 34 presses, nine more than before.
4. For 30 presses the digit sum must be 30 − 9 = 21 or 30 − 18 = 12 or 3, since each trade adds 9.
5. Largest 3-digit number: 993, with the digit sum 21: (8 × 100) + (19 × 10) + (3 × 1) = 993 uses 8 + 19 + 3 = 30 presses.
6. Smallest 3-digit number: 102, with the digit sum 3: (8 × 10) + (22 × 1) = 102 uses 8 + 22 = 30 presses.
Answer: 997 in 34 presses too; largest 993 and smallest 102 with exactly 30 presses

concepts.concept_name: Fewest button presses

content.text:
Systematic Sippy is a different kind of calculator. It has the following buttons: +1, +10, +100, +1000, +10000, +100000. It wants to be used as minimally as possible.
How can we get the numbers (a) 5072, (b) 8300 using as few button clicks as possible? Find out which buttons should be clicked and how many times to get the desired numbers given in the table. The aim is to click as few buttons as possible.
Here is one way to get the number 5072. This method uses 23 button clicks in total.
Is there another way to get 5072 using less than 23 button clicks? Write the expression for the same.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 5072 made with 5 presses of +1000, 6 of +10 and 12 of +1 takes 23 presses. Can it be done in fewer?
2. Ten presses of one button can always be traded for one press of the next bigger button, which saves nine presses.
3. So every button except the biggest is pressed at most nine times: the presses are the digits.

content.text:
Worked example: Make (a) 5072 and (b) 8300 with the fewest button presses. One way to get 5072 takes 5 + 0 + 6 + 12 = 23 presses.
1. (a) 5072 = (5 × 1000) + (0 × 100) + (7 × 10) + (2 × 1): the presses are the digits 5, 0, 7 and 2.
2. Number of presses: 5 + 7 + 2 = 14, which is fewer than 23.
3. (b) 8300 = (8 × 1000) + (3 × 100).
4. Number of presses: 8 + 3 = 11.
Answer: (a) (5 × 1000) + (7 × 10) + (2 × 1) in 14 presses; (b) (8 × 1000) + (3 × 100) in 11 presses

concepts.concept_name: Ten lakhs make a crore

content.text:
What if we press the +10,00,000 button ten times? What number will come up? How many zeroes will it have? What should we call it?
The number will be 100 lakhs, which is also called a crore. 1 crore is written as 1,00,00,000, it is 1 followed by seven zeroes.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q1 (fewest presses)

content.book_number: Figure it Out, Q1 (fewest presses)
content.question: For the numbers in the previous exercise, find out how to get each number by making the smallest number of button clicks and write the expression. The numbers are (a) 8300 (b) 40629 (c) 56354 (d) 66666 (e) 367813.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q2 (a connection)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q2 (a connection): Do you see any connection between each number and the corresponding smallest number of button clicks?
1. Take the number 8300: its digits are 8, 3, 0 and 0, and 8 + 3 + 0 + 0 = 11 is its smallest number of clicks.
2. 40629 has digits adding to 4 + 0 + 6 + 2 + 9 = 21, the smallest clicks.
3. 56354 gives 5 + 6 + 3 + 5 + 4 = 23, and 66666 gives 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30.
4. 367813 gives 3 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 1 + 3 = 28.
5. So the smallest number of clicks is the sum of the digits of the number.
Answer: The smallest number of clicks is the sum of the digits of the number

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q3 (why the expression is the place value notation)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q3 (why the expression is the place value notation): If you notice, the expressions for the least button clicks also give the Indian place value notation of the numbers. Think about why this is so.
1. Ten presses of one button make the same amount as one press of the next bigger button.
2. So in the fewest way no button other than the biggest is pressed ten or more times.
3. Each press count is then a single digit from 0 to 9, written in that button's place.
4. Written side by side, these counts are the digits of the number in place value notation, for example 5072 has 5 thousands, 0 hundreds, 7 tens and 2 ones.
Answer: Each place holds at most nine presses, so the counts are the digits of the number

concepts.concept_name: Two comma patterns

content.text:
1.3 Of Crores and Crores!
The table below shows some numbers according to both the Indian system and the American system (also called the International system) of naming numerals and placing commas. Observe the placement of commas in both systems.
Indian system: 1,000 One thousand; 10,000 Ten thousand; 1,00,000 One lakh; 10,00,000 Ten lakhs; 1,00,00,000 One crore; 10,00,00,000 Ten crores; 1,00,00,00,000 One arab or One hundred crores.
American system: 1,000 One thousand; 10,000 Ten thousand; 100,000 Hundred thousand; 1,000,000 One million; 10,000,000 Ten million; 100,000,000 Hundred million; 1,000,000,000 One billion.
Notice that in the Indian system, commas are placed to group the digits in a 3-2-2-2... pattern from right to left (thousands, lakhs, crores, etc.). In the American system, the digits are grouped uniformly in a 3-3-3-3... pattern from right to left (thousands, millions, billions, etc.).
The Indian system of naming numbers is also followed in Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Maldives, Afghanistan, and Myanmar. The words lakh and crore originate from the Sanskrit words lakṣha and koṭi. The American system is also used in many countries.

content.text:
1. Predict first: where do the commas go in 10,00,000 in the Indian system, and where in 1,000,000 in the American system?
2. Indian: the first comma comes after 3 digits from the right, then after every 2 digits.
3. American: a comma after every 3 digits from the right.
4. Ten lakh is one million, one crore is ten million, and one hundred crore is one billion.

content.text:
Worked example: Place commas in 12345678 in the Indian and the American system and read it in both.
1. Indian system, groups of 3 then 2s: the last three digits 678, then 45, then 23, then 1.
2. So 12345678 is 1,23,45,678: one crore twenty three lakh forty five thousand six hundred seventy eight.
3. American system, groups of 3: 678, then 345, then 12.
4. So 12345678 is 12,345,678: twelve million three hundred forty five thousand six hundred seventy eight.
Answer: Indian 1,23,45,678; American 12,345,678

concepts.concept_name: Zeros in a lakh, a crore and an arab

content.text:
Observe the number of zeroes in 1 lakh and 1 crore. 1 lakh, written in numbers would be 1 followed by 5 zeroes. 1 crore, written in numbers would be 1 followed by 7 zeroes.
A lakh is a hundred times a thousand, a crore is a hundred times a lakh and an arab is a hundred times a crore (i.e., a hundred thousand is 1 lakh, 100 lakhs is 1 crore, and 100 crores is 1 arab).
How many zeros does a thousand lakh have? ____
How many zeros does a hundred thousand have? ____

content.text:
Worked example: Show that a lakh is a hundred thousands, a crore a hundred lakhs and an arab a hundred crores. Then find the zeros in a thousand lakh and in a hundred thousand.
1. A lakh: 100 × 1000 = 1,00,000, with 5 zeros.
2. A crore: 100 × 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,000, with 7 zeros.
3. An arab: 100 × 1,00,00,000 = 1,00,00,00,000, with 9 zeros.
4. A thousand lakh: 1000 × 1,00,000 = 10,00,00,000, which has 8 zeros and is ten crore.
5. A hundred thousand: 100 × 1000 = 1,00,000, which has 5 zeros and is one lakh.
Answer: A thousand lakh has 8 zeros; a hundred thousand has 5 zeros

concepts.concept_name: Reading a ten-digit number in both systems

content.text:
The number 9876501234 can be easily read by placing commas first:
(a) 9,87,65,01,234 → 9 arab 87 crore 65 lakhs 1 thousand and 234 or 987 crore 65 lakh 1 thousand 234 (in the Indian system).
(b) 9,876,501,234 → 9 billion 876 million 501 thousand 234 (in the American system).
We shall come across even bigger numbers in later grades.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students compare the Indian 3-2-2 grouping with the international 3-3-3 grouping, and write the same number with commas and name it in both systems.
Students say that a lakh is a hundred thousands, a crore is a hundred lakhs and an arab is a hundred crores, count the zeros in each, and find the zeros in a thousand lakh and in a hundred thousand.
Students place commas in 9876501234 in both systems and read it as arab, crore and lakh in the Indian system and as billion, million and thousand in the international system.
Students place commas in both systems, name each part with lakh, crore, million or billion, and convert between the names by multiplying and dividing by 10 lakh.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q1 (read and name in both systems)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q1 (read and name in both systems): Read the following numbers in Indian place value notation and write their number names in both the Indian and American systems: (a) 4050678 (b) 48121620 (c) 20022002 (d) 246813579 (e) 345000543 (f) 1020304050
1. (a) Indian 40,50,678: forty lakh fifty thousand six hundred seventy eight. American 4,050,678: four million fifty thousand six hundred seventy eight.
2. (b) Indian 4,81,21,620: four crore eighty one lakh twenty one thousand six hundred twenty. American 48,121,620: forty eight million one hundred twenty one thousand six hundred twenty.
3. (c) Indian 2,00,22,002: two crore twenty two thousand two. American 20,022,002: twenty million twenty two thousand two.
4. (d) Indian 24,68,13,579: twenty four crore sixty eight lakh thirteen thousand five hundred seventy nine. American 246,813,579: two hundred forty six million eight hundred thirteen thousand five hundred seventy nine.
5. (e) Indian 34,50,00,543: thirty four crore fifty lakh five hundred forty three. American 345,000,543: three hundred forty five million five hundred forty three.
6. (f) Indian 1,02,03,04,050: one arab two crore three lakh four thousand fifty. American 1,020,304,050: one billion twenty million three hundred four thousand fifty.
Answer: (a) 40,50,678 (b) 4,81,21,620 (c) 2,00,22,002 (d) 24,68,13,579 (e) 34,50,00,543 (f) 1,02,03,04,050, each named in both systems as shown

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q2 (names to numerals)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q2 (names to numerals): Write the following numbers in Indian place value notation: (a) One crore one lakh one thousand ten (b) One billion one million one thousand one (c) Ten crore twenty lakh thirty thousand forty (d) Nine billion eighty million seven hundred thousand six hundred
1. (a) 1 crore, 01 lakh, 01 thousand, 010: 1,01,01,010.
2. (b) One billion one million one thousand one is 1,001,001,001. In the Indian system this is 1,00,10,01,001.
3. (c) 10 crore, 20 lakh, 30 thousand, 040: 10,20,30,040.
4. (d) Nine billion eighty million seven hundred thousand six hundred is 9,080,700,600. In the Indian system this is 9,08,07,00,600.
Answer: (a) 1,01,01,010 (b) 1,00,10,01,001 (c) 10,20,30,040 (d) 9,08,07,00,600

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q3 (compare)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q3 (compare): Compare and write '<', '>' or '=': (a) 30 thousand ____ 3 lakhs (b) 500 lakhs ____ 5 million (c) 800 thousand ____ 8 million (d) 640 crore ____ 60 billion
1. (a) 30 thousand is 30 × 1000 = 30,000 and 3 lakhs is 3 × 1,00,000 = 3,00,000. So it is <.
2. (b) 500 lakhs is 500 × 1,00,000 = 5,00,00,000 and 5 million is 5 × 10,00,000 = 50,00,000. So it is >.
3. (c) 800 thousand is 800 × 1000 = 8,00,000 and 8 million is 8 × 10,00,000 = 80,00,000. So it is <.
4. (d) 640 crore is 640 × 1,00,00,000 = 6,40,00,00,000 and 60 billion is 60 × 1,00,00,00,000 = 60,00,00,00,000. So it is <.
Answer: (a) < (b) > (c) < (d) <

concepts.concept_name: Rounding up and rounding down

content.text:
1.4 Exact and Approximate Values
1 lakh people visited the book fair. "Ohh, so many people!" "If I had not gone, they would have written 99,999 people visited the book fair last week".
What do you think of this conversation? Have you read or heard such headlines or statements?
Very often, exact numbers are not required and just an approximation is sufficient. For example, according to the 2011 census, the population of Chintamani town is 76,068. Instead, saying that the population is about 75,000 is enough to give an idea of how big the quantity is.
Bappi, call and check if Toofan Express is on time. "What number did you call?" "I called the rounded off number, of course! My teacher told us that efficient people deal with rounded off numbers."
There are situations where it makes sense to round up a number (rounding up is when the approximated number is more than the actual number). For example, if a school has 732 people including students, teachers and staff: the principal might order 750 sweets instead of 700 sweets.
There are situations where it is better to round down (rounding down is when the approximated number is less than the actual number). For example, if the cost of an item is ₹470, the shopkeeper may say that the cost is around ₹450 instead of saying it is around ₹500.
Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding up or rounding down is okay and (d) when exact numbers are needed.

1 lakh people visited the book fair. "Ohh, so many people!" "If I had not gone, they would have written 99,999 people visited the book fair last week".
What do you think of this conversation? Have you read or heard such headlines or statements?

Very often, exact numbers are not required and just an approximation is sufficient. For example, according to the 2011 census, the population of Chintamani town is 76,068. Instead, saying that the population is about 75,000 is enough to give an idea of how big the quantity is.
Bappi, call and check if Toofan Express is on time. "What number did you call?" "I called the rounded off number, of course! My teacher told us that efficient people deal with rounded off numbers."

There are situations where it makes sense to round up a number (rounding up is when the approximated number is more than the actual number). For example, if a school has 732 people including students, teachers and staff: the principal might order 750 sweets instead of 700 sweets.

There are situations where it is better to round down (rounding down is when the approximated number is less than the actual number). For example, if the cost of an item is ₹470, the shopkeeper may say that the cost is around ₹450 instead of saying it is around ₹500.
Think and share situations where it is appropriate to (a) round up, (b) round down, (c) either rounding up or rounding down is okay and (d) when exact numbers are needed.

content.text:
Worked example: A school has 732 people and the principal orders sweets. An item costs 470 rupees and the shopkeeper says around 450 rupees. Which one rounds up and which rounds down? Give one situation for each of: round up, round down, either, exact.
1. 732 is more than 700, so an order of 700 sweets leaves 732 − 700 = 32 people without.
2. 750 is more than 732, so ordering 750 rounds up and every person gets a sweet.
3. 450 is less than 470, so saying around 450 rounds down; 470 − 450 = 20 rupees less.
4. Round up: buying food for a group. Round down: the time left to catch the school bus.
5. Either: the distance between two far away places. Exact: handling money in a bank.
Answer: Ordering 750 rounds up; saying around 450 rounds down; the four situations are given above

content.text:
Worked example: Find all numbers whose five nearest neighbours are all 5,00,00,000, and say how many there are.
1. The nearest thousand is the strictest: the number must be within half a thousand of 5,00,00,000.
2. The smallest such number is 5,00,00,000 − 500 = 4,99,99,500, which rounds up.
3. The largest is 5,00,00,000 + 499 = 5,00,00,499, since 5,00,00,500 rounds up to 5,00,01,000.
4. Count: 5,00,00,499 − 4,99,99,500 + 1 = 1000.
5. These numbers also round to 5,00,00,000 at ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore.
Answer: All numbers from 4,99,99,500 to 5,00,00,499; there are 1000 of them

media.description: A number has five crore as its nearest neighbour at the thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore. learning_objectives.objective_text: Students tell the difference between an exact and an approximate value, say when rounding up or down suits a situation, and give situations where an exact number is needed.
Students round a large number to the nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore by looking at the digit to the right of the place, and write the five nearest neighbours of two numbers.
Students find the numbers whose nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore are all 5,00,00,000, and count how many there are by using the tightest neighbour.
Students place a number on a number line, see which neighbour it is closer to, and write all five nearest neighbours of a number.

concepts.concept_name: Estimating a sum

content.text:
Roxie and Estu are estimating the values of simple expressions.
1. 4,63,128 + 4,19,682. Roxie: "The sum is near 8,00,000 and is more than 8,00,000." Estu: "The sum is near 9,00,000 and is less than 9,00,000."
(a) Are these estimates correct? Whose estimate is closer to the sum?
(b) Will the sum be greater than 8,50,000 or less than 8,50,000? Why do you think so?
(c) Will the sum be greater than 8,83,128 or less than 8,83,128? Why do you think so?
(d) Exact value of 4,63,128 + 4,19,682 = ____

content.text:
1. Predict first: is the sum nearer to 8,00,000 or to 9,00,000?
2. Round each part, add, and decide whether the real sum is more or less by seeing which way each part was rounded.
3. Compare each part with a benchmark part: if both parts are bigger than the benchmark parts, the sum is bigger.

content.text:
Worked example: Check the estimates of 4,63,128 + 4,19,682 by Roxie (near 8,00,000, more) and Estu (near 9,00,000, less). Say whose is closer, whether the sum is above or below 8,50,000 and 8,83,128, and find the exact sum.
1. Roxie rounds down both parts to 4,00,000 + 4,00,000 = 8,00,000, so the sum is more than that.
2. Estu rounds up to 5,00,000 + 4,00,000 = 9,00,000, so the sum is less than that. Both are correct.
3. (d) The exact sum is 4,63,128 + 4,19,682 = 8,82,810.
4. Distance from 9,00,000: 9,00,000 − 8,82,810 = 17,190. Distance from 8,00,000: 8,82,810 − 8,00,000 = 82,810. Estu is closer.
5. (b) 4,63,128 is more than 4,50,000 and 4,19,682 is more than 4,00,000, so the sum is more than 8,50,000.
6. (c) 8,83,128 is 4,63,128 + 4,20,000. Since 4,19,682 is less than 4,20,000, the sum is less than 8,83,128.
Answer: Both estimates are correct; Estu's is closer; more than 8,50,000; less than 8,83,128; exact sum 8,82,810

Worked example: Write a general observation about the table and an appropriate title.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the population of Pune in 2011 and approximately how much it grew from 2001. Then find the city whose population grew the most.
1. Pune in 2011: 31,15,431, which is about 31 lakh. In 2001: 25,38,473, about 25 lakh.
2. Approximate increase: 31 lakh − 25 lakh = 6 lakh. The exact increase is 31,15,431 − 25,38,473 = 5,76,958.
3. Look for large jumps: Bengaluru 84,25,970 − 43,01,326 = 41,24,644.
4. Hyderabad grew by 31,72,487, Ahmedabad by 20,50,500 and Surat by 20,33,962, all less than Bengaluru.
5. So Bengaluru grew the most, by 41,24,644.
Answer: Pune: 31,15,431 in 2011, grew by about 6 lakh. Bengaluru grew the most, by 41,24,644

content.text:
Worked example: Find the cities whose population nearly doubled, and the number by which Patna's population is multiplied to come close to Mumbai's.
1. Bengaluru: about 43 lakh in 2001, twice is about 86 lakh, and 2011 is about 84 lakh. Close to double.
2. Hyderabad: 36 lakh doubled is 72 lakh, and 2011 is 68 lakh. Surat: 24 lakh doubled is 48 lakh, and 2011 is about 45 lakh.
3. Vadodara: 17 lakh doubled is 34 lakh, and 2011 is about 36 lakh.
4. Ahmedabad (55 lakh against 70 lakh) and Pimpri-Chinchwad (17 lakh against 20 lakh) are not close.
5. Patna is about 17 lakh and Mumbai is about 124 lakh. Now 7 × 17 = 119 and 8 × 17 = 136, so about 7.
6. Exact: 1,24,42,373 ÷ 16,84,222 is about 7.39.
Answer: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Surat and Vadodara nearly doubled; multiply Patna's population by about 7.39

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students read the table of twenty cities, write an observation about the change from 2001 to 2011, and give the table a suitable title.
Students round two populations to lakhs to find an approximate increase for Pune, and compare increases to find the city whose population grew the most.
Students decide which cities nearly doubled by checking that the 2011 value is close to twice the 2001 value, and find by what number Patna's population is multiplied to come near Mumbai's.
Students pick two columns of a table, subtract to find an increase, divide to see how many times, and write an observation from the numbers.

content.text:
1.5 Patterns in Products
Roxie and Estu are playing with multiplication. They encounter an interesting technique for multiplying a number by 10, 100, 1000, and so on.
A Multiplication Shortcut
Roxie evaluated 116 × 5 as follows: 116 × 5 = (116 × 10) ÷ 2 = 1160 ÷ 2 = 580.
Estu evaluated 824 × 25 as follows: 824 × 25 = (824 × 100) ÷ 4 = 82,400 ÷ 4 = 20,600.

1. 116 × 10 = 1160.
2. 1160 ÷ 2 = 580, so 116 × 5 = 580.
3. 824 × 100 = 82,400.
4. 82,400 ÷ 4 = 20,600, so 824 × 25 = 20,600.
Answer: 116 × 5 = 580 and 824 × 25 = 20,600

Ten in each group is twice as many as five in each group, so 8 × 5 is half of 8 × 10.
Dividing by 2 and multiplying by 10 scales by 10 ÷ 2, which is 5.

content.text:
Worked example: Explain why a number times 5 is the number times 10 divided by 2, using 8 × 5.
1. 8 × 10 means 8 groups of 10, which is 80.
2. 5 is half of 10, so each group has half as many.
3. So 8 × 5 is half of 80, which is 40.
4. In general, 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so n × 5 = (n × 10) ÷ 2.
5. Dividing first also works: (8 ÷ 2) × 10 = 40.
Answer: 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so times 5 is times 10 then halve, e.g. 8 × 5 = 40

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q1 (quick products)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q1 (quick products): Find quick ways to calculate these products: (a) 2 × 1768 × 50 (b) 72 × 125 [Hint: 125 = 1000 ÷ 8] (c) 125 × 40 × 8 × 25
1. (a) Pair 2 and 50 to make 100. Then 1768 × 100 = 1,76,800.
2. (b) 125 is 1000 ÷ 8. So 72 × 125 = (72 × 1000) ÷ 8. 72,000 ÷ 8 = 9000.
3. (c) Pair 125 with 8 to make 1000, and 40 with 25 to make 1000. Then 1000 × 1000 = 10,00,000.
Answer: (a) 1,76,800 (b) 9000 (c) 10,00,000

concepts.concept_name: Patterns in products

content.text:
How Long is the Product?
In each of the following boxes, the multiplications produce interesting patterns. Evaluate them to find the pattern. Extend the multiplications based on the observed pattern.

Box two: 66 × 61, 666 × 661, 6666 × 6661.
Box three: 3 × 5, 33 × 35, 333 × 335.
Box four: 101 × 101, 102 × 102, 103 × 103.

concepts.concept_name: Roxie's claim about 2-digit numbers

content.text:
Observe the number of digits in the two numbers being multiplied and their product in each case. Is there any connection between the numbers being multiplied and the number of digits in their product?
Roxie says that the product of two 2-digit numbers can only be a 3- or a 4-digit number. Is she correct?
Should we try all possible multiplications with 2-digit numbers to tell whether Roxie's claim is true? Or is there a better way to find out?
She explains her reasoning: "We want to know about the number of digits in the product of two 2-digit numbers. To know the smallest such product I took 10 × 10, so all other products will be greater than 100. To know the greatest such product I multiplied the smallest 3-digit numbers (100 × 100) to get 10,000; so the product of all the 2-digit multiplications will be less than 10,000."
Can multiplying a 3-digit number with another 3-digit number give a 4-digit number?
Can multiplying a 4-digit number with a 2-digit number give a 5-digit number?

1. Predict first: is the largest product of two 2-digit numbers, 99 × 99, below 10,000?
2. The smallest product comes from the smallest numbers and the largest product from the largest numbers, so two checks cover every case.
3. Check the smallest and the largest products for each pair of digit counts.

content.text:
Worked example: Is Roxie right that two 2-digit numbers give a 3-digit or 4-digit product? Can two 3-digit numbers give a 4-digit product? Can a 4-digit number times a 2-digit number give a 5-digit product?
1. Smallest: 10 × 10 = 100, which has 3 digits.
2. Largest: 99 × 99 = 9801, which has 4 digits.
3. Every other product lies between them, so Roxie is right.
4. Two 3-digit numbers: the smallest is 100 × 100 = 10,000, which already has 5 digits. So never 4 digits.
5. A 4-digit and a 2-digit number: the smallest is 1000 × 10 = 10,000, which has 5 digits, so yes.
6. The largest is 9999 × 99 = 9,89,901, which has 6 digits.
Answer: Roxie is right; two 3-digit numbers never give 4 digits; a 4-digit times a 2-digit number can give 5 digits (or 6)

concepts.concept_name: The digit-count rule

content.text:
Observe the multiplication statements below. Do you notice any patterns? See if this pattern extends for other numbers as well.
A 1-digit number times a 1-digit number gives a 1-digit or 2-digit number.
A 2-digit number times a 1-digit number gives a 2-digit or 3-digit number.
A 2-digit number times a 2-digit number gives a 3-digit or 4-digit number.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a 2-digit times a 2-digit gives 3 or 4 digits. What is 2 + 2, and what is one fewer?
2. The smallest m-digit number is 1 followed by m − 1 zeros, and the smallest product is 1 followed by m + n − 2 zeros, which has m + n − 1 digits.
3. The largest product is below the smallest (m + n)-digit number, so the product has at most m + n digits.

content.text:
Worked example: Fill in the table: 5-digit times 5-digit, 8-digit times 3-digit, and 12-digit times 13-digit. State the rule.
1. For a 1-digit number times a 1-digit number the counts are 1 and 2: 1 + 1 − 1 = 1 and 1 + 1 = 2.
2. A 5-digit number times a 5-digit number gives 5 + 5 − 1 = 9 or 5 + 5 = 10 digits.
3. An 8-digit number times a 3-digit number gives 8 + 3 − 1 = 10 or 8 + 3 = 11 digits.
4. A 12-digit number times a 13-digit number gives 12 + 13 − 1 = 24 or 12 + 13 = 25 digits.
5. Rule: an m-digit number times an n-digit number has m + n − 1 or m + n digits.
Answer: 9 or 10; 10 or 11; 24 or 25 digits. The rule is m + n − 1 or m + n digits

Students test Roxie's claim that two 2-digit numbers give a product of 3 or 4 digits by using the smallest and largest numbers, and decide whether two 3-digit numbers give 4 digits and whether 4-digit and 2-digit numbers give 5.

Students predict the number of digits in a product from the digit counts of the two numbers, check the prediction with the smallest and the largest numbers, and decide when each count can occur.

concepts.concept_name: Facts hidden in products

content.text:
Fascinating Facts about Large Numbers
Some interesting facts about large numbers are hidden below. Calculate the product or quotient to uncover the facts. Once you find the product or quotient, read the number in both Indian and American naming systems. Share your thoughts and questions about the fact with the class after you discover each number.
1250 × 380 is the number of kirtanas composed by Purandaradasa according to legends. Purandaradasa was a composer and singer in the 15th century. His kirtanas spanned social reform, bhakti and spirituality. He systematised methods for teaching Carnatic music which is followed to the present day. How many years did he live to compose so many songs? At what age did he start composing songs? If he composed 4,75,000 songs, how many songs per year did he have to compose?
2100 × 70,000 is the approximate distance in kilometres between the Earth and the Sun. This distance keeps varying throughout the year. The farthest distance is about 152 million kilometres. How did they measure the distance between the Earth and the Sun?
6400 × 62,500 is the average number of litres of water the Amazon river discharges into the Atlantic Ocean every second. The river's flow into the Atlantic is so much that drinkable freshwater is found even 160 kilometres into the open sea.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 1250 × 380, 2100 × 70,000 and 6400 × 62,500, and name each in both systems.
1. 1250 × 380 = 4,75,000: four lakh seventy five thousand in the Indian system, and four hundred seventy five thousand in the American system.
2. 2100 × 70,000 = 14,70,00,000: fourteen crore seventy lakh, or one hundred forty seven million.
3. 6400 × 62,500 = 40,00,00,000: forty crore, or four hundred million.
4. To ask how long Purandaradasa composed, suppose he composed for 50 years. Then 4,75,000 ÷ 50 = 9,500 songs a year.
5. The Earth to Sun distance is about 14,70,00,000 km, which is about 147 million km.
Answer: 4,75,000; 14,70,00,000; 40,00,00,000 (named in both systems above)

concepts.concept_name: Facts hidden in quotients

content.text:
As you did before, divide the given numbers to uncover interesting facts about division. Share your thoughts and questions with the class after you uncover each number.
13,95,000 ÷ 150 is the distance (in kms) of the longest single-train journey in the world. The train runs in Russia between Moscow and Vladivostok. The duration of this journey is about 7 days. The longest train route in India is from Dibrugarh in Assam to Kanyakumari in Tamil Nadu; it covers 4219 kms in about 76 hours.
Adult blue whales can weigh more than 10,50,00,000 ÷ 700 kilograms. A newborn blue whale weighs around 2,700 kg, which is similar to the weight of an adult hippopotamus. Blue whales can eat up to 3500 kg of krill every day.
52,00,00,00,000 ÷ 130 was the weight, in tonnes, of global plastic waste generated in the year 2021.
Large Number Fact: In a single gram of healthy soil there can be 100 million to 1 billion bacteria and 1 lakh to 1 million fungi, which can support plants' growth and health.
Share such large-number facts you know / come across with your class.

concepts.concept_name: Could Mumbai fit into buses and ships

content.text:
1.6 Did You Ever Wonder...?
Estu is amused by all these interesting facts about large numbers. He came up with an unusual question, "Could the entire population of Mumbai fit into 1 lakh buses?" What do you think? How can we find out?
Let us assume a bus can accommodate 50 people. Then 1 lakh buses can accommodate 1 lakh × 50 = 50 lakh people.
The population of Mumbai is more than 1 crore 24 lakhs (we saw this in an earlier table). So, the entire population of Mumbai cannot fit in 1 lakh buses.
The RMS Titanic ship carried about 2500 passengers. Can the population of Mumbai fit into 5000 such ships?

lines: 1.6 Did You Ever Wonder...?

Estu is amused by all these interesting facts about large numbers. He came up with an unusual question, "Could the entire population of Mumbai fit into 1 lakh buses?" What do you think? How can we find out?
Let us assume a bus can accommodate 50 people. Then 1 lakh buses can accommodate 1 lakh × 50 = 50 lakh people.
The population of Mumbai is more than 1 crore 24 lakhs (we saw this in an earlier table). So, the entire population of Mumbai cannot fit in 1 lakh buses.
The RMS Titanic ship carried about 2500 passengers. Can the population of Mumbai fit into 5000 such ships?

content.text:
1. Predict first: one lakh buses of 50 people each. Is that more or less than one crore people?
2. State the assumption, multiply, and compare with the population of Mumbai.
3. A fit needs a capacity at least as big as the population.

content.text:
Worked example: Could Mumbai's population, 1,24,42,373, fit into 1 lakh buses of 50 people each? Could it fit into 5000 ships of 2500 people each?
1. 1,00,000 × 50 = 50,00,000 people in the buses.
2. 50,00,000 is less than 1,24,42,373, so no.
3. 5000 × 2500 = 1,25,00,000 people in the ships.
4. 1,25,00,000 − 1,24,42,373 = 57,627, so the ships have room for 57,627 more people than the city.
5. So yes, 5000 such ships could carry everyone.
Answer: No for the buses (50,00,000 is too few); yes for the ships (1,25,00,000 is more)

concepts.concept_name: Reaching the Moon and the Sun

content.text:
Inspired by this strange question, Roxie wondered, "If I could travel 100 kilometers every day, could I reach the Moon in 10 years?" (The distance between the Earth and the Moon is 3,84,400 km.)
How far would she have travelled in a year? How far would she have travelled in 10 years?
Is it not easier to perform these calculations in stages? You can use this method for all large calculations.
Find out if you can reach the Sun in a lifetime, if you travel 1000 kilometers every day. (You had written down the distance between the Earth and the Sun in a previous exercise.)

content.text:
Worked example: At 100 km a day, how far is a year and ten years, and can Roxie reach the Moon (3,84,400 km)?
1. In a year: 100 × 365 = 36,500 km.
2. In ten years: 36,500 × 10 = 3,65,000 km.
3. 3,84,400 − 3,65,000 = 19,400, so she is 19,400 km short of the Moon.
Answer: 36,500 km in a year; 3,65,000 km in 10 years; 19,400 km short of the Moon

concepts.concept_name: Reaching the Moon and the Sun

content.text:
Worked example: At 1000 km a day, can you reach the Sun, 14,70,00,000 km away, in a lifetime of 100 years?
1. Days needed: 14,70,00,000 ÷ 1000 = 1,47,000 days.
2. Days in 100 years: 365 × 100 = 36,500, which is less than 1,47,000.
3. Years needed: 1,47,000 ÷ 365 is about 402.7 years.
4. So no, a lifetime is not enough.
Answer: 1,47,000 days, about 402.7 years, so not in a lifetime

concepts.concept_name: Sheets, babies and coins

content.text:
Make necessary reasonable assumptions and answer the questions below:
(a) If a single sheet of paper weighs 5 grams, could you lift one lakh sheets of paper together at the same time?
(b) If 250 babies are born every minute across the world, will a million babies be born in a day?
(c) Can you count 1 million coins in a day? Assume you can count 1 coin every second.
Think and create more such fun questions and share them with your class.

concepts.concept_name: Sheets, babies and coins

content.text:
Worked example: 250 babies are born every minute. Are a million babies born in a day? Can you count a million coins in a day at one coin every second?
1. Babies in a day: 250 × 60 × 24 = 3,60,000.
2. 3,60,000 is less than 10,00,000, so no.
3. Seconds in a day: 60 × 60 × 24 = 86,400, so only 86,400 coins can be counted.
4. 86,400 is less than 10,00,000, so no.
Answer: No for both: 3,60,000 babies and 86,400 coins in a day

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students assume a bus holds 50 people, find the people in one lakh buses, compare with Mumbai's population, and test 5000 ships of 2500 people.
Students work out the distance travelled in a year and in ten years at 100 km a day, compare with the distance to the Moon, and find the days needed to reach the Sun at 1000 km a day.
Students make stated assumptions and test whether one lakh sheets of paper can be lifted, whether a million babies are born in a day, and whether a million coins can be counted in a day.
Students solve the book's closing questions on large numbers by stating the assumption, working in stages and judging whether the answer is reasonable.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q1 (ten digits once each)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q1 (ten digits once each): Using all digits from 0 to 9 exactly once (the first digit cannot be 0) to create a 10-digit number, write the (a) largest multiple of 5 (b) smallest even number.
1. A multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5. For the largest, put the digits in the biggest order, which ends with 0: 9876543210.
2. An even number ends in an even digit. The smallest start is 1, then 0, then the other digits in order.
3. That order is 1023456789, but it ends in 9, which is odd.
4. Swap the last two digits to end with 8: 1023456798. This is the smallest even number.
Answer: (a) 9876543210 (b) 1023456798

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q2 (the longest name)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q2 (the longest name): The number 10,30,285 in words is Ten lakhs thirty thousand two hundred eighty five, which has 42 letters. Give a 7-digit number name which has the maximum number of letters.
1. Use the same style of naming as the book, with the plural in ten lakhs.
2. Choose the lakh digits, the thousand digits and the last three digits so that each part has a long word.
3. Seventy seven lakhs seventy seven thousand seven hundred seventy seven is 77,77,777. It has 61 letters.
4. Checking all 7-digit numbers by computer gives 61 as the maximum, reached by 81 numbers; 73,73,373 is the smallest of them.
Answer: The largest number of letters is 61, for example 77,77,777

steps: Use the same style of naming as the book, with the plural in ten lakhs.

Seventy seven lakhs seventy seven thousand seven hundred seventy seven is 77,77,777. It has 61 letters.
Checking all 7-digit numbers by computer gives 61 as the maximum, reached by 81 numbers; 73,73,373 is the smallest of them.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q3 (swap and get bigger)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q3 (swap and get bigger): Write a 9-digit number where exchanging any two digits results in a bigger number. How many such numbers exist?
1. Exchanging two digits makes the number bigger only if the smaller digit is on the left.
2. So every digit must be smaller than all the digits to its right: the digits increase from left to right.
3. The digits must be different, and zero cannot lead. The only choice is the nine digits 1 to 9 in increasing order.
4. So the number is 1,23,45,67,89 and it is the only one.
Answer: 1,23,45,67,89; exactly one such number

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q4 (strike out ten digits)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q4 (strike out ten digits): Strike out 10 digits from the number 12345123451234512345 so that the remaining number is as large as possible.
1. The number has 20 digits, so 10 digits remain.
2. Put the largest digit first. Strike out the four digits 1, 2, 3, 4 in front of the first 5.
3. Strike out the next four digits 1, 2, 3, 4 so that a second 5 follows. That is 8 digits struck.
4. Two strikes remain. Strike out the next 1 and 2 so that 3 comes next.
5. What remains is 5534512345.
Answer: 5534512345

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q5 (letters shared by number names)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q5 (letters shared by number names): The words 'zero' and 'one' share letters 'e' and 'o'. The words 'one' and 'two' share a letter 'o', and the words 'two' and 'three' also share a letter 't'. How far do you have to count to find two numbers, one after the other, which do not share an English letter in common?
1. Write each number name and compare it with the next one.
2. Names like nineteen and twenty share n, t and e. Ninety nine and one hundred share n and e.
3. Checking every pair of neighbours up to three million, in the Indian and the international spelling, finds no pair without a shared letter.
4. So there may be no such pair at all; the search turns up none.
Answer: No such pair was found, however far we count

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q6 (digits written one after the other)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q6 (digits written one after the other): Suppose you write down all the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, ..., 9, 10, 11, ... The tenth digit you write is '1' and the eleventh digit is '0', as part of the number 10. (a) What would the 1000th digit be? At which number would it occur? (b) What number would contain the millionth digit? (c) When would you have written the digit '5' for the 5000th time?
1. Count the digits by length: numbers 1 to 9 use 9 digits, 10 to 99 use 90 × 2 = 180 digits, so 189 digits in all, and 3-digit numbers use 900 × 3 = 2700 digits.
2. (a) 1000 − 189 = 811 digits into the 3-digit numbers. 811 ÷ 3 gives 270 whole numbers and 1 left over. So the digit is the first digit of the 271st 3-digit number, 100 + 270 = 370. The digit is 3, in 370.
3. (b) Up to 5-digit numbers: 9 + 180 + 2700 + 36,000 + 4,50,000 = 4,88,889 digits. The millionth digit is 10,00,000 − 4,88,889 = 5,11,111 digits into the 6-digit numbers. 5,11,111 ÷ 6 gives 85,185 whole numbers and 1 left over. So it is the first digit of 1,00,000 + 85,185 = 1,85,185, and the digit is 1.
4. (c) Counting the fives written by computer, the digit 5 is written for the 5000th time in the number 13,495.
Answer: (a) 3, in the number 370 (b) 1,85,185 (c) at the number 13,495

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q7 (two buttons)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q7 (two buttons): A calculator has only '+10,000' and '+100' buttons. Write an expression describing the number of button clicks to be made for the following numbers: (a) 20,800 (b) 92,100 (c) 1,20,500 (d) 65,30,000 (e) 70,25,700
1. Use as many +10,000 presses as fit, then press +100 for the rest.
2. (a) 20,800 = (2 × 10,000) + (8 × 100). Clicks: 2 + 8 = 10.
3. (b) 92,100 = (9 × 10,000) + (21 × 100). Clicks: 9 + 21 = 30.
4. (c) 1,20,500 = (12 × 10,000) + (5 × 100). Clicks: 12 + 5 = 17.
5. (d) 65,30,000 = 653 × 10,000. Clicks: 653.
6. (e) 70,25,700 = (702 × 10,000) + (57 × 100). Clicks: 702 + 57 = 759.
Answer: (a) 10 (b) 30 (c) 17 (d) 653 (e) 759 clicks

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q8 (lakhs in a billion)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q8 (lakhs in a billion): How many lakhs make a billion?
1. A billion is 100 crore, and a crore is 100 lakh.
2. So a billion is 100 × 100 lakh = 10,000 lakh.
3. Check: 10,000 × 1,00,000 = 1,00,00,00,000, which is 1 followed by 9 zeros.
Answer: 10,000 lakhs make a billion

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q9 (two sets of cards)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q9 (two sets of cards): You are given two sets of number cards numbered from 1 to 9. Place a number card in each box below to get the (a) largest possible sum (b) smallest possible difference of the two resulting numbers. The boxes are a row of 7 boxes on top and a row of 5 boxes below, lined up on the right.
1. Each digit 1 to 9 can be used twice, so 18 cards are available.
2. (a) For the largest sum put the largest digits in the highest places of both numbers: 99,87,654 on top and 87,654 below.
3. The sum is 99,87,654 + 87,654 = 1,00,75,308.
4. (b) For the smallest difference make the top number as small as possible and the bottom number as large as possible: 11,22,334 on top and 99,887 below.
5. The difference is 11,22,334 − 99,887 = 10,22,447.
Answer: (a) 1,00,75,308 (b) 10,22,447

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q11 (coins to match a statue)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q11 (coins to match a statue): Find out how many coins should be stacked to match the height of the Statue of Unity. Assume each coin is 1 mm thick.
1. The Statue of Unity is about 180 metres tall.
2. 1 metre is 1000 mm, so 180 m = 180 × 1000 mm = 1,80,000 mm.
3. Each coin is 1 mm, so 1,80,000 coins are needed.
Answer: 1,80,000 coins

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q12 (an albatross trip)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q12 (an albatross trip): Grey-headed albatrosses have a roughly 7-feet wide wingspan. They are known to migrate across several oceans. Albatrosses can cover about 900 to 1000 km in a day. One of the longest single trips recorded is about 12,000 km. How many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean approximately?
1. Days = distance ÷ distance each day.
2. At 1000 km a day: 12,000 ÷ 1000 = 12 days.
3. At 900 km a day: 12,000 ÷ 900 is about 13.3 days.
4. So the trip takes about 12 to 14 days.
Answer: About 12 to 14 days

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q13 (a godwit's flight)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q13 (a godwit's flight): A bar-tailed godwit holds the record for the longest recorded non-stop flight. It travelled 13,560 km from Alaska to Australia without stopping. Its journey started on 13 October 2022 and continued for about 11 days. Find out the approximate distance it covered every day. Find out the approximate distance it covered every hour.
1. Distance each day = 13,560 ÷ 11, which is about 1233 km.
2. A day has 24 hours, so the distance each hour is 1233 ÷ 24, which is about 51 km.
Answer: About 1233 km each day and about 51 km each hour

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out, Q14 (heights against Somu's building)

content.text:
Figure it Out, Q14 (heights against Somu's building): Bald eagles are known to fly as high as 4500 to 6000 m above the ground level. Mount Everest is about 8850 m high. Aeroplanes can fly as high as 10,000 to 12,800 m. How many times bigger are these heights compared to Somu's building?
1. Somu's building is 40 m tall.
2. Eagles: 4500 ÷ 40 = 112.5 and 6000 ÷ 40 = 150. So about 112 to 150 times.
3. Mount Everest: 8850 ÷ 40 = 221.25, so about 221 times.
4. Aeroplanes: 10,000 ÷ 40 = 250 and 12,800 ÷ 40 = 320. So 250 to 320 times.
Answer: Eagles 112.5 to 150 times, Everest about 221 times, aeroplanes 250 to 320 times

media.title: Which nine digit numbers get bigger when any two digits are exchanged?
media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A nine digit number must grow whenever any two of its digits change places. One exchange is studied to see when the number grows, and that rule is applied to every pair of places. The number found is tested with two exchanges.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a place on the left is worth more, so an exchange grows the number only when the left digit is the smaller one. Watch for students who forget that equal digits give the same number, and that the first digit cannot be zero.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

nine increasing digits chosen from 0 to 9 omit one digit; if 0 is used it is first, which is not allowed, so 0 is omitted
the number is 123456789, written 12,34,56,789 in lakh and crore grouping, and it is the only one

video_script.substitution: Write the names of two neighbours side by side and mark the letters they share; look first for a shared whole word.

final_answer.value: No such pair was found in the numbers checked
final_answer.spoken: no pair without a shared letter turns up in all the numbers we checked

maths_rules: zero and one share e and o; one and two share o; two and three share t
forty seven and forty eight share the whole word forty
nineteen (n, i, e, t) and twenty (t, w, e, n, y) share n, e, t; ninety nine and one hundred share n and e
nine hundred ninety nine and one thousand share letters such as n, e, t, h, u, d

every pair of neighbours up to 30,00,000 (3 million), in the Indian names and the international names, shares at least one letter; the search stops there, so it shows no pair, which is not a proof for every number
video_script.design: One idea: compare neighbouring names letter by letter. The four names stay in the anchor band; the working band builds the comparisons. The answer says what the search shows and no more. No hard clear.
open_questions: The book (and the worklist) say no such pair is found 'however far we count'. A search of every neighbouring pair up to thirty lakh, in the Indian and the international spelling, finds no pair without a shared letter, but that is not a proof for every number, so the answer says 'in the numbers checked'.

media.description: The counting numbers are written one after another and the digits are counted group by group. The thousandth digit, the number holding the millionth digit and the place of the five thousandth five are all found by counting in groups.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: count the digits in groups by length of number, and stop when the total reaches the target. Watch for students who forget the left-over digits, which show where inside a number the target digit falls.

video_script.why: The child can read and compare large numbers, and now counts the digits of the counting numbers in groups by length.
video_script.substitution: Count the digits group by group (one digit numbers, two digit numbers, and so on); divide what is left by the length of the next group; the left-over digits show the place inside the number.

final_answer.spoken: the thousandth digit is three, in the number three hundred seventy

maths_rules: digits up to 99: 9 + 180 = 189; 1000 - 189 = 811; 811 / 3 = 270 remainder 1; the 271st three digit number is 100 + 270 = 370; its first digit is 3

fives: in 1 to 9999 each of 4 places holds 5 in 1000 numbers, so 4000; in each of 10,000 to 10,999, 11,000 to 11,999, 12,000 to 12,999 three places hold 5 in 100 numbers each, so 300 for each thousand, 900 in all; total 4900 by 12,999

from 13,000 each block of 100 numbers has 10 fives in the ones place and 10 in the tens place, so 20; 13,000 to 13,399 give 80; total 4980; the last 20 fives come in 13,400 to 13,495: 13405, 13415, 13425, 13435, 13445, 13450 to 13459 (13455 has two), 13465, 13475, 13485, 13495; the 20th is the ones digit of 13,495
video_script.design: One idea: count digits by groups and stop at the target. The long row of digits stays in the anchor band; the working band builds three counts one below another. The fives count is shown by hand grouping, not as a computer count. No hard clear.
open_questions: The book answer key gives 13,995 for the fives question; the worklist and a direct count give 13,495. The video follows 13,495 and shows the hand grouping.

media.title: How many days does an albatross take to cross an ocean?
media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A trip of twelve thousand kilometres is divided by the distance flown each day, once for the fastest day and once for the slowest day. The two answers give a range of days, and each end is checked by multiplying back.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: days equal the distance divided by the distance flown each day, so a range of daily distances gives a range of days. Watch for students who round thirteen and a bit down to thirteen, when the bird is still flying on the fourteenth day.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many days does an albatross take to cross an ocean?
source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text, opened only after the student tries the question
items: Grey-headed albatrosses have a roughly 7-feet wide wingspan. They are known to migrate across several oceans. Albatrosses can cover about 900 to 1000 km in a day. One of the longest single trips recorded is about 12,000 km. How many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean approximately?
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child divides a long distance by a distance for one day, and now does it for a range of daily distances to get a range of days.

interaction_points.prompt: About how many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean?
interaction_points.answer: About 12 to 14 days
covers: Grey-headed albatrosses have a roughly 7-feet wide wingspan. They are known to migrate across several oceans. Albatrosses can cover about 900 to 1000 km in a day. One of the longest single trips recorded is about 12,000 km. How many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean approximately?

source: Grey-headed albatrosses have a roughly 7-feet wide wingspan. They are known to migrate across several oceans. Albatrosses can cover about 900 to 1000 km in a day. One of the longest single trips recorded is about 12,000 km. How many days would such a trip take to cross an ocean approximately?
video_script.why: The child divides a long distance by a distance for one day, and now does it for a range of daily distances to get a range of days.
video_script.substitution: Divide the trip distance by the fastest and by the slowest distance flown each day, and read the two answers as a range.
video_script.anchor: a grey-headed albatross over an ocean, with the trip of 12,000 km marked along the water
video_script.payoff_line: Divide the distance by the distance flown each day, once for each speed

final_answer.value: About 12 to 14 days

maths_rules: days = distance / distance flown each day
at 1000 km each day: 12,000 / 1000 = 12 days
at 900 km each day: 12,000 / 900 = 13.33 days, a little more than 13, so the trip runs into the 14th day
video_script.design: One idea: a range of daily distances gives a range of days. The albatross and the trip stay in the anchor band; the working band shows the two divisions and the checks. No hard clear.
open_questions: The exact range is 12 to 13.33 days; the worklist and the book say about 12 to 14 days. The video follows the book and explains that thirteen and a bit days runs into the fourteenth day.

content.text:
Toothpick Digits
We can write digits as shown in the image below. You can either use toothpicks or matchsticks, or just write the digits in this way, using lines to represent sticks.
To make the digit 7, three sticks are needed.
Write or make the number 5108. How many sticks are required?
1. Make or write the number 42,019. It would require exactly 23 sticks.
2. Starting with 42,019, add or write two more sticks, and make a bigger number. One example is 42,078. What other numbers bigger than 42,019 can you make in this way?

content.text:
Worked example: Count the sticks in 5108 and in 42,019. Then add exactly two sticks to 42,019 to make bigger numbers.
1. 5108 uses 5 + 2 + 6 + 7 = 20 sticks.
2. 42,019 uses 4 + 5 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 23 sticks.
3. Changing 0 to 8, 1 to 7 or 9 to 8 each adds one stick. Any two of these give 42,879, 42,818 or 42,078.
4. Changing 1 to 4, 2 to 8 or 4 to 9 adds two sticks. These give 42,049, 48,019 and 92,019.
5. A new digit 1 uses exactly two sticks, so 1,42,019 is also bigger.
Answer: 5108 needs 20 sticks; 42,019 needs 23; for example 42,049, 42,078, 42,818, 42,879, 48,019, 92,019

2. The digit 1 uses 2 sticks, so many 1s make the longest number. The digit 8 uses 7 sticks, so few 8s make the shortest number.
3. A number is smaller when it has fewer digits, so look for the fewest digits that can hold 24 sticks.

content.text:
Worked example: Make a number using exactly 24 sticks. Find the biggest and the smallest such numbers.
1. Example: 2008 uses 5 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 24 sticks.
2. Biggest: use the cheapest digit 1 as many times as possible, 24 ÷ 2 = 12 times, and 12 digits make the longest number: 1,11,11,11,11,111.
3. Smallest: three digits hold at most 3 × 7 = 21 sticks, which is under 24, so four digits are needed.
4. The first digit should be as small as possible: 1 uses 2 sticks and leaves 22, more than the 21 that three digits can hold. The next choice is 2 with 5 sticks, leaving 19, and 0, 0, 8 uses 6 + 6 + 7 = 19.
5. So the smallest is 2008.
Answer: Example 2008; biggest 1,11,11,11,11,111; smallest 2008

media.title: Biggest and smallest number from twenty four sticks
media.context: Large Numbers Around Us. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: An example, the biggest number and the smallest number are made with exactly twenty four sticks. The biggest comes from the cheapest digit used as often as possible, and the smallest from the fewest digits with the smallest digit first. Keeko raises the doubt that the biggest digits make the biggest number.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: more digits make a bigger number, so the cheapest digit gives the biggest number and the fewest digits give the smallest. Watch for students who pick the biggest digits instead of counting digits first.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

final_answer.spoken: twelve ones in a row for the biggest, and two thousand eight for the smallest

maths_rules: 2008 uses 5 + 6 + 6 + 7 = 24 sticks
biggest: each digit needs at least 2 sticks, so at most 24 / 2 = 12 digits, and 12 digits at 2 sticks each are all 1s: 1,11,11,11,11,111 (twelve ones)
smallest: three digits hold at most 3 x 7 = 21 sticks, under 24, so four digits are needed
first digit: 1 uses 2 and leaves 22, more than 21 that three digits hold; 2 uses 5 and leaves 19 = 6 + 6 + 7, so 2, 0, 0, 8
the slip: 9, 9, 9, 9 use 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 sticks and make 9999, but it has only four digits
video_script.design: One idea: more digits make a bigger number. The stick digits stay in the anchor; the working band builds the example, then the biggest, then the smallest. Keeko's doubt: the biggest digits make the biggest number.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about large numbers

content.text:
Summary
We came across large numbers, lakhs, crores and arabs; millions and billions. We learnt how to read and write these numbers in the Indian and American/International naming systems.
(a) 1 lakh is 1 followed by 5 zeroes: 1,00,000
(b) 1 crore is 1 followed by 7 zeroes: 1,00,00,000
(c) 1 million is 1 followed by 6 zeroes: 1,000,000 (which is also ten lakhs)
(d) 1 arab is 1 followed by 9 zeroes: 1,000,000,000 (which is also 100 crore or 1 billion)
We generally round up or round down large numbers. Many times it is enough just to know roughly how big or small something is.
To get a sense of large numbers or quantities, we can check how many times bigger they are compared to numbers or quantities that are more familiar.
We saw how to factorise numbers and regroup them to make multiplications simpler.
We carried out interesting thought experiments such as, "Would one be able to watch 1000 movies in a year?"

content.text:
1. Estu's question is settled: 100 years of tasting one variety a day is 36,500, and three a day passes one lakh.
2. A lakh has five zeros, a crore seven, an arab nine; ten lakh is a million.
3. Still open for you: would you be able to watch 1000 movies in a year? State your assumption and test it.
