objectives.objective_text: Students name the largest and smallest numbers with three to six digits, add one to the largest five-digit number, and read 1,00,000 as one lakh.
Students write the days in y years as 365 times y, work out the varieties tasted in 100 years for one, two and three varieties a day, and compare each with one lakh.
Students place a number on a ruler marked at one lakh, say how much less or more than one lakh it is, and find the change between two populations by subtracting.
Students find the height of a ten-floor building from the height of one floor, find how much taller a statue and a waterfall are, and count the floors needed to match the waterfall.
Students check Roxie's lakh-days and lakh-people claims by calculation, quote Estu's reasons that a lakh can look small, and say why big or small depends on the comparison.
Students compare a tall height with a building of floors, say how many times taller it is, and judge a big number against a real thing.
Students place commas in the Indian system, read a number as lakhs, thousands and the rest, and write the number name of a number such as 12,78,830.
Students turn a number name into digits by writing each part in its place, with zeros where a place is empty and commas in the Indian system.
Students drop digits into a place value ladder, place the Indian-system commas, and read the number as lakhs, thousands and the rest.
Students divide a number by 1000 to find the presses of a plus-1000 button, and multiply the presses by 1000 to find the number shown.
Students divide a number by 10 to find the presses of a plus-10 button, and see that counting in tens needs ten times as many presses as counting in hundreds.
Students divide by 100 to find the presses of a plus-100 button, and decide whether Handy Hundreds can show numbers that Tedious Tens and Thoughtful Thousands cannot.
Students pick the calculator that shows a given number, count its presses by dividing, and say which other calculators can show the same number.
Students write a number such as 5072 as button presses of place values in a second and a third way, and check each expression adds to the number.
Students trade a press of a larger button for ten presses of the next one, see that each trade adds nine presses, and use it to make 997 in two ways and the extreme 3-digit numbers in 30 presses.
Students trade presses between place value buttons on a board, write an expression for each way to make a number, and check that each expression adds to the target.
Students make 5072 and 8300 with as few presses as possible by using each digit as the presses of its place value button, and compare with a longer way.
Students press the plus ten lakh button ten times, read the number as 100 lakhs, and write it as 1 followed by seven zeros named a crore.
Students find the least number of presses for a number by reading its digits, compare the count with the sum of the digits, and explain why the expression matches the Indian place value notation.
Students compare the Indian 3-2-2 grouping with the international 3-3-3 grouping, and write the same number with commas and name it in both systems.
Students say that a lakh is a hundred thousands, a crore is a hundred lakhs and an arab is a hundred crores, count the zeros in each, and find the zeros in a thousand lakh and in a hundred thousand.
Students place commas in 9876501234 in both systems and read it as arab, crore and lakh in the Indian system and as billion, million and thousand in the international system.
Students place commas in both systems, name each part with lakh, crore, million or billion, and convert between the names by multiplying and dividing by 10 lakh.
Students tell the difference between an exact and an approximate value, say when rounding up or down suits a situation, and give situations where an exact number is needed.
Students round a large number to the nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore by looking at the digit to the right of the place, and write the five nearest neighbours of two numbers.
Students find the numbers whose nearest thousand, ten thousand, lakh, ten lakh and crore are all 5,00,00,000, and count how many there are by using the tightest neighbour.
Students place a number on a number line, see which neighbour it is closer to, and write all five nearest neighbours of a number.
Students test two estimates of 4,63,128 + 4,19,682, decide which is closer, argue whether the sum is above or below 8,50,000 and 8,83,128, and find the exact sum.
Students test two estimates of 14,63,128 − 4,90,020, decide which is closer, argue whether the difference is above or below 9,50,000 and 9,63,128, and find the exact difference.
Students estimate a sum or difference by rounding, say whether the real value is above or below the estimate, and check against the exact value.
Students read the table of twenty cities, write an observation about the change from 2001 to 2011, and give the table a suitable title.
Students round two populations to lakhs to find an approximate increase for Pune, and compare increases to find the city whose population grew the most.
Students decide which cities nearly doubled by checking that the 2011 value is close to twice the 2001 value, and find by what number Patna's population is multiplied to come near Mumbai's.
Students pick two columns of a table, subtract to find an increase, divide to see how many times, and write an observation from the numbers.
Students multiply 116 by 5 by multiplying by 10 and halving, and multiply 824 by 25 by multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4.
Students explain using the meaning of multiplication and division why multiplying by 5 matches multiplying by 10 and dividing by 2.
Students regroup the factors of a product into tens, hundreds and thousands by halving and doubling, and use the regrouping to find products quickly.
Students evaluate three boxes of multiplications, spot the pattern in each box, and extend each pattern to a larger multiplication.

Students test Roxie's claim that two 2-digit numbers give a product of 3 or 4 digits by using the smallest and largest numbers, and decide whether two 3-digit numbers give 4 digits and whether 4-digit and 2-digit numbers give 5.
Students read the table of digit counts, state that an m-digit number times an n-digit number has m plus n or m plus n minus one digits, and apply it to three new pairs.
Students predict the number of digits in a product from the digit counts of the two numbers, check the prediction with the smallest and the largest numbers, and decide when each count can occur.
Students multiply 1250 by 380, 2100 by 70,000 and 6400 by 62,500, and read each product in the Indian and the American naming systems.
Students divide 13,95,000 by 150, 10,50,00,000 by 700 and 52,00,00,00,000 by 130, read each quotient in both systems, and read the soil fact with million and billion.
Students multiply or divide to uncover a large number fact, read the result in both systems, and ask a question about it.
Students assume a bus holds 50 people, find the people in one lakh buses, compare with Mumbai's population, and test 5000 ships of 2500 people.
Students work out the distance travelled in a year and in ten years at 100 km a day, compare with the distance to the Moon, and find the days needed to reach the Sun at 1000 km a day.
Students make stated assumptions and test whether one lakh sheets of paper can be lifted, whether a million babies are born in a day, and whether a million coins can be counted in a day.
Students solve the book's closing questions on large numbers by stating the assumption, working in stages and judging whether the answer is reasonable.
Students restate how a lakh, a crore, a million and an arab are written, when to round, how to feel the size of a number, and one thought experiment from the chapter.
